notes.meaning: Pilate ordered Jesus to be severely flogged with a Roman whip. He did this hoping that a lesser punishment would satisfy the angry crowd so he could let Jesus go. Flogging an innocent person showed a weak governor willing to compromise justice to keep the peace.

Roman soldiers twisted sharp thorns into a crown and jammed it onto Jesus' head, then threw a purple robe over His bleeding shoulders. They knelt before Him in mock respect, hailed Him as King of the Jews, and repeatedly struck Him in the face. Their cruel game showed deep contempt, yet Jesus bore their shame and cruelty with quiet patience.

Pilate went back outside to speak to the religious leaders and the gathered crowd. He announced that he was bringing Jesus out so everyone could see he found no basis for any legal charge against Him. Pilate hoped that seeing Jesus bruised and bleeding would convince them that justice had been satisfied.

Jesus stepped outside wearing the painful crown of thorns and the royal purple robe, His body covered with bleeding wounds. Pilate presented Him to the crowd and said, 'Here is the man!' He meant to show that this battered, harmless prisoner was no dangerous rebel to be feared.

When the chief priests and temple guards saw Jesus, they showed no pity and immediately screamed for His crucifixion. Pilate told them in sharp frustration to take Him and crucify Him themselves, repeating that he found no crime in Him. Pilate knew the Jewish leaders lacked the legal authority to execute anyone on their own, but he was losing control of the situation.

The Jewish leaders revealed their real reason for wanting Jesus dead when the charge of rebellion against Rome failed to work. They claimed that according to the Law of Moses, Jesus had to die for blasphemy—which means speaking evil of God or claiming His divine rights. By declaring Himself to be the Son of God, Jesus was claiming to be equal with God Himself.

When Pilate heard that Jesus claimed to be the Son of God, his dread grew even deeper. As a Roman, he was superstitious and feared that he might be dealing with a god who had come down in human form. His troubled conscience and the fear of punishing a divine person made him hesitate to carry out the crowd's wishes.

Pilate went back inside the governor's headquarters and asked Jesus, 'Where are You from?' He was not asking about Jesus' earthly hometown, but whether His origin was human or divine. Jesus gave no answer because Pilate already knew He was innocent yet refused to stand up for the truth.

Offended by Jesus' silence, Pilate demanded to know why the prisoner would not speak to him. He proudly reminded Jesus that he held the official authority either to release Him or to crucify Him. Pilate believed his high Roman rank gave him complete control over Jesus' life and death.

Jesus calmly answered that Pilate would have no power at all unless God had granted it from heaven. Earthly rulers govern only within the limits God permits, and Pilate was acting as an instrument in God's eternal plan. Even so, the religious leaders who handed Jesus over were guilty of a greater sin because they possessed God's law and acted out of pure malice.

Struck by Jesus' words, Pilate tried even harder to find a way to set Him free. The Jewish leaders countered by shouting that anyone who made himself a king was an enemy of Caesar, the Roman emperor. Knowing that Emperor Tiberius was intensely suspicious and cruel, Pilate was terrified of being accused of treason and losing his position.

Giving in to the political threats, Pilate brought Jesus outside to conclude the trial. He sat down on the official stone judgment seat in an open-air area called Gabbatha, which means an elevated place. From this formal platform, Roman governors spoke with full imperial authority to deliver binding legal verdicts.

It was Friday, the preparation day for the Passover Sabbath, during the middle of the morning. Pilate presented Jesus to the people and said sarcastically, 'Here is your King!' In his bitter mockery of the Jewish crowd, Pilate unknowingly pointed out the true King of Israel while the festival lambs were being prepared.

other.label: Catholic
other.view: The Catholic commentator Cornelius à Lapide reports a view that Pilate gave in at the third hour and then formally passed sentence at the sixth.

notes.meaning: The crowd shouted furiously to take Jesus away and crucify Him. When Pilate asked if he should crucify their King, the chief priests answered that they had no king but Caesar. In their desperate hatred of Jesus, the religious leaders abandoned their national faith and rejected God's rule over their nation.

Pilate finally gave up and handed Jesus over to be crucified according to their demands. The Roman soldiers took charge of Jesus and led Him away toward the execution ground. The innocent Savior was led like a lamb to the slaughter, taking the path to the cross for the rescue of sinners.

In keeping with Roman custom, Jesus was forced to carry His own heavy wooden crossbeam as He walked. He was led out of the city gates to an execution site called Golgotha, which means the Place of the Skull. Dying outside the city walls fulfilled the Old Testament picture of the sin offering carried outside the camp.

At Golgotha, the soldiers nailed Jesus to the cross between two criminals, with Jesus placed in the middle. Putting Him between two thieves treated Him as the worst criminal of the group. This fulfilled the ancient prophecy that the Messiah would be numbered among lawbreakers in His death.

Pilate ordered a written sign to be nailed to the top of the cross to declare the crime. It read: 'Jesus of Nazareth, the King of the Jews.' Although Pilate meant the title as an insult to the Jewish authorities, God used the governor's pen to proclaim Jesus' true, everlasting kingship over all.

Many people read the notice because the crucifixion site sat close to the city near a well-traveled road. Pilate had the words written in Hebrew, Latin, and Greek—the local, imperial, and worldwide languages of the day. This ensured that visitors and travelers from across the ancient world could read and understand the proclamation.

The chief priests were outraged that the sign named Jesus as their actual king instead of an impostor. They went to Pilate and urged him to change the wording to say only that Jesus claimed to be the King of the Jews. They could not stand having their rejected Messiah publicly announced as their ruler before the entire world.
